title: The Cold Cover
premise: Jonah Joubert, an analyst fired from three intelligence agencies for refusing to falsify findings, now works off-books cases for a broker who deals in deniability. When a regional flight disappears from every tracking system while still airborne—yet lands safely, with passengers who remember nothing—Jonah realizes the erasure was a rehearsal for something larger: a staged disaster meant to be blamed on a dead whistleblower, erasing both a plane and a truth. Following memory fragments from a passenger who starts recalling what was done to the cabin, Jonah traces the operation to a private security firm selling 'narrative hygiene' to a defense contractor. In the climax aboard a second targeted flight, Jonah forces the plane to land by triggering the very paper trail the plotters erased, exposing them at the cost of their last shred of anonymity. The ending finds Jonah, finally visible and finally believed, choosing to stay in the light rather than vanish again.
about_author: J. M. Underhill is the pen name of a former aviation-industry analyst who spent a decade inside the paperwork of things that never officially happened. They write from a coastal town where fog is frequent and records, they insist, are never quite what they seem.

chapters.title: Unattributed
chapters.summary: POV Jonah. Fired, broke, and working from a laundromat back office, Jonah takes a case no agency will touch: a grieving sister insists her brother's flight landed with the wrong man in his seat. The beat is weary resignation—Jonah has learned that invisibility is safety, and this case threatens both. A single anomaly hooks them: the flight's tracking data simply stops, then resumes, mid-air.

chapters.title: The Gap Over Water
chapters.summary: POV Jonah. Jonah reconstructs the flight from radar hobbyists and a retired controller, confirming an eleven-minute gap in every official record. The sister, Amara, gives them her brother's voicemail from the plane—his voice slurred, confused, saying the cabin 'smelled like oranges.' Emotional beat: the first flare of purpose Jonah has felt in years, and the fear that comes with it.

chapters.title: Passenger 14C
chapters.summary: POV alternating Jonah and Mara Voss, a passenger from the flight who begins having intrusive memories—hypodermic stings, a masked crew member, orange scent. Jonah finds her through the manifest and realizes she's being followed. Beat: uneasy alliance. Two people who shouldn't trust anyone choosing to, because memory is the only evidence left.

chapters.title: Narrative Hygiene
chapters.summary: POV Jonah. Following the orange scent—a proprietary sedative—Jonah uncovers Halcyon Risk Group, a firm selling 'incident management' to corporations: make disasters look like accidents, or make them look like nothing at all. Jonah's old agency contact warns them off, then quietly slips them a file. Beat: dread deepening; the scale of the erasure is institutional, not criminal.

chapters.title: What the Whistleblower Knew
chapters.summary: POV Mara. Mara's memories sharpen: the 'crew' rehearsed, filmed, and photographed the sedation. She recalls a name—Elias Renner, a dead engineer who'd accused a defense contractor of falsifying safety data. Beat: grief and violation. Mara realizes her mind was turned into a crime scene, and that recovering it is an act of defiance.

chapters.title: Three Agencies, Three Fires
chapters.summary: POV Jonah. The plotters retaliate by leaking Jonah's fabricated personnel files, painting them as unstable—a preemptive erasure of the investigator. Old colleagues shun them; the broker drops the case. Beat: the novel's darkest hour for identity—Jonah confronts how much of themselves they surrendered to stay invisible, and decides visibility is worth the risk.

chapters.title: The Second Flight
chapters.summary: POV Jonah. Decoding Halcyon's scheduling patterns, Jonah identifies the real target: a charter carrying the contractor's own internal auditors, scheduled to 'fail' over mountains in four days, blamed on Renner's posthumous sabotage. Beat: cold clarity. The rehearsal wasn't a one-off; it was calibration, and the countdown has started.

chapters.title: Paper Against Metal
chapters.summary: POV Mara. Mara agrees to board the charter as a planted passenger, carrying a recorder and a sedative-detection kit, her recovered memories as her only weapon. Beat: terror and resolve. In a quiet scene she records a message for her daughter in case the plane doesn't land—choosing, for the first time, to be remembered rather than safe.

chapters.title: Eleven Minutes
chapters.summary: POV Jonah, intercut with Mara. The sedation attempt begins mid-flight; Mara triggers the alarm and Jonah, on the ground, floods every channel—regulators, newsrooms, the contractor's own board—with the un-erased paper trail in real time. The crew aborts; the plane diverts and lands. Beat: white-knuckle climax where documentation itself becomes the rescue.

chapters.title: The Visible Woman, the Visible Man
chapters.summary: POV Jonah, closing with Mara. Halcyon's principals are arrested; the first flight's passengers are told the truth, most choosing to forget it anyway—except Mara, who testifies. Jonah, offered reinstatement, declines and instead goes on record under their own name. Beat: resolution and quiet triumph. Belonging, the novel argues, begins the moment you stop hiding.
